title: Ship an AI summariser that is right 82% of the time?
summary: The model is good, not reliable. Decide what accuracy is enough, for whom, and how the product should behave when it is wrong.

brief.role: You are the PM for a clinical operations product.
brief.company: Aldercroft, a 180-person company selling shift-handover software to hospital operations teams (not clinical decision support).
brief.context: The team has built an AI summariser that condenses a shift's operational notes — bed availability, staffing gaps, equipment issues, escalations — into a handover summary. Evaluated against 400 human-written summaries, it produces an acceptable summary 82% of the time. Of the 18% failures, most are omissions; about 3% of all summaries invent a detail not present in the notes. Launch is proposed for next month. Your head of clinical safety has not signed off. The CEO has told an investor the feature ships this quarter.
brief.objective: Decide whether and how to ship, given that this sits next to clinical work without being clinical decision support.
brief.constraints: The evaluation set is 400 summaries from 6 hospitals. Improving accuracy meaningfully is estimated at one to two quarters. The feature is already built and behind a flag.
brief.task: Decide what ships, to whom, and what the product does about the 18%.

evidenceCards.title: Evaluation results
evidenceCards.content:
400 shift summaries from 6 hospitals, each scored by two experienced charge nurses against the source notes.

Acceptable (would hand over as-is or with trivial edits): 82%
Omission of a material item: 15%
  — of which: staffing gaps 6%, equipment issues 5%, escalations 3%, bed status 1%
Fabricated detail not in the source notes: 3%
  — examples: named a ward that had no notes that shift; stated a piece of equipment was 'repaired' when the note said 'reported'

Human baseline: the same nurses reviewed 100 human-written handover summaries against source notes. 91% acceptable; 9% had material omissions; 0% fabrications.

Evaluation caveat from the data scientist: '400 summaries, 6 hospitals, and the two reviewers agreed on the rating 87% of the time. The 3% fabrication rate has a confidence interval of roughly 1.6% to 5.2%. All 6 hospitals are UK NHS trusts of similar size; I would not assume this transfers to a US or private setting.'

evidenceCards.title: How handover actually works today
evidenceCards.content:
Observation study, 11 handovers across 3 hospitals:

- Handover is verbal, supported by written notes. The written summary is a reference during and after the conversation, not a replacement for it.
- Median time spent writing the summary: 12 minutes at the end of a shift, usually while the nurse is already over their hours. Every participant described it as the worst part of the shift.
- In 9 of 11 handovers, the incoming nurse asked clarifying questions that surfaced items not in the written summary. Omissions in the written record are normal and the verbal handover is where they get caught.
- 2 of 11: the written summary was the only handover, because of staffing. Both were night-to-day transitions in the same hospital.
- Nurses' stated concern when shown the feature: 'If it writes it for me, will anyone read the notes?' Several said they would still read the source notes; two said they probably would not after a hard shift.

Researcher's note: 'The verbal conversation is a strong error-correcting layer, but it is not always present.'

evidenceCards.title: Clinical safety and regulatory position
evidenceCards.content:
From the head of clinical safety:
'This product is not a medical device and I want to keep it that way. The moment we present a generated summary as an authoritative clinical record, we are in a different regulatory category and a different liability position.

My concerns, in order:
1. Fabrication is categorically worse than omission here. An omission gets caught in the verbal handover. A confident false statement about equipment being repaired does not get questioned, because it reads like a fact someone recorded.
2. Automation bias is real and documented. If the summary looks complete, review effort falls.
3. I am not against shipping. I am against shipping it as a finished summary with no visible provenance.

What would get my signature: the output is clearly a draft, every claim is traceable to a source note, the nurse edits and confirms before it is saved, and we log edit rates so we can see whether review is actually happening.'

evidenceCards.title: Commercial and competitive context
evidenceCards.content:
Two competitors have announced AI summarisation. One shipped three months ago; a customer of theirs told your account team it is 'switched off in most wards because it made things up'. The other has announced but not shipped.

Your pipeline: 7 open opportunities mention AI summarisation as a requirement or a strong interest, roughly $1.9m. Three of those are US private hospital groups.

The CEO told an investor on the last call that the feature ships this quarter. There is no contractual commitment to any customer.

Time saved if it works: 12 minutes per nurse per shift. At a mid-size trust that is roughly 40 hours a week of nursing time. Every hospital operations director shown a prototype has reacted strongly positively to that number.

Customer advisory board (9 hospitals) asked about AI features: 7 said they would want a human confirmation step; 2 said they would want it fully automatic to get the full time saving.

decisionPrompt: What do you ship next month, and how does the product handle the cases where the model is wrong?

decisionOptions.label: Ship as a reviewed draft with per-claim provenance and edit logging
decisionOptions.description: The summary appears as a pre-filled draft, each line links to the source note it came from, the nurse edits and confirms before it is saved, and edit rates are logged and monitored.
decisionOptions.consequence:
Clinical safety signs off in two weeks. The feature ships to all customers a week later than proposed.
Measured over the first quarter: median summary time falls from 12 minutes to 5. Edit rate is 34% of summaries in month one, falling to 22% by month three — which the team watches carefully as a possible automation-bias signal rather than an improvement.
Two fabrications are caught by nurses and reported through the in-product flag; both are traced to ambiguous source notes and used to improve the prompt. None reach a handover.
Four of the seven pipeline opportunities close. The CEO's quarter commitment is met.
Trade-off: you gave up most of the theoretical time saving to keep a human in the loop, and you now have to monitor a declining edit rate that may or may not mean something bad.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Strongest when the rationale distinguishes omission from fabrication, uses the verbal handover as an existing but unreliable error-correcting layer, and treats the declining edit rate as a risk to monitor rather than a success metric.

decisionOptions.label: Ship the summariser as-is with a disclaimer
decisionOptions.description: 82% is close to the 91% human baseline. Ship the generated summary as the summary, with a notice that it is AI-generated and should be checked.
decisionOptions.consequence:
The feature ships on the proposed date and the time saving is real — summary time falls to under two minutes.
In week five a fabricated line stating that a ventilator had been repaired appears in a handover at a hospital where the night-to-day transition is written-only. The incoming team acts on it. No patient is harmed; the incident is reported and investigated by the trust.
The feature is switched off by that trust and two others. Your head of clinical safety escalates to the board. The relaunch, with provenance and confirmation, happens four months later into a much more sceptical customer base.
Trade-off: you took the full time saving and the full risk, in the one part of the workflow that has no error-correcting layer.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Weak. It compares 82% to 91% as if the failure modes were equivalent, ignores that humans fabricate at 0%, and ignores the two of eleven handovers with no verbal layer.

decisionOptions.label: Hold the launch and spend a quarter improving accuracy
decisionOptions.description: Do not ship at 82%. Spend one to two quarters raising accuracy, particularly eliminating fabrication, then revisit.
decisionOptions.consequence:
A quarter of work moves acceptable summaries from 82% to 89% and fabrication from 3% to 1.4%. That is real progress and the confidence interval on fabrication still includes 2%.
The CEO's investor commitment is missed and has to be walked back on the next call. Two of the seven opportunities go to the competitor whose product 'makes things up', which your account team finds frustrating.
When the feature finally ships, it ships as a reviewed draft with provenance anyway — because at 1.4% fabrication the head of clinical safety's position is unchanged. The team observes that the design change, not the accuracy work, was what unblocked the launch.
Trade-off: you improved the model, missed the window, and discovered the blocker was the interaction design rather than the accuracy number.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Defensible caution. Mark down when the rationale treats accuracy as the only lever and never considers that product design can change the consequence of an error.

decisionOptions.label: Ship to a small pilot of hospitals with heavy instrumentation
decisionOptions.description: Release the reviewed-draft version to three hospitals for a quarter, measure fabrication rates and edit behaviour in the field, then decide about general availability.
decisionOptions.consequence:
Three hospitals opt in. Over a quarter the field fabrication rate comes in at 2.1%, close to the evaluation, and the edit-rate decline is observed clearly enough to design a mitigation for.
The data is genuinely better than the lab evaluation. The cost is a quarter of delay for the other customers, the CEO's commitment is missed, and two pipeline opportunities stall.
General availability follows with a better product and a much stronger evidence base for the US expansion, where the data scientist had warned the evaluation may not transfer.
Trade-off: you bought real-world evidence at the price of the quarter, and the safeguards you piloted were available to everyone from day one.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Strong risk instinct. Credit the field-evidence argument and the US transferability concern. Mark down when it does not weigh that the same safeguards could ship broadly at the same time.

rubric.referenceReasoning: The 82% against a 91% human baseline invites the wrong comparison, because the two failure modes are not equivalent. Humans omit; the model omits and also fabricates at around 3%, and humans fabricate at 0%. Omissions are caught by the verbal handover, which the observation study shows is a real error-correcting layer — except in the 2 of 11 cases where there is no verbal handover at all, which is exactly where a confident false statement would land unchallenged. That reframes the problem: the lever is not only accuracy, it is what the product does around the error. The head of clinical safety has already described a design that changes the consequence of a fabrication — draft framing, per-claim provenance, explicit confirmation, edit-rate logging — and that design is available now, at 82%, without a quarter of model work. A strong answer separates the two failure modes, notices that design changes the risk more cheaply than accuracy does, and treats the falling edit rate as automation bias to monitor rather than as evidence of improvement.
evidenceSignals: Distinguishes omission from fabrication and treats them as different risks
Notes humans omit at 9% but fabricate at 0%, so 82% vs 91% is not the right comparison
Uses the verbal handover as an error-correcting layer and notices the 2 of 11 cases without one
Reads the fabrication confidence interval (1.6%-5.2%) rather than the point estimate
Notices the evaluation is 6 similar UK trusts and may not transfer to US private hospitals
Sees that the head of clinical safety named a shippable design, not a blocking objection

product_sense: Reframes the question from 'is the model accurate enough' to 'what happens when it is wrong'
Recognises that interaction design can change the consequence of a model error more cheaply than model work can
Notices the automation-bias concern the nurses raised themselves
analytics: Uses the confidence interval on the fabrication rate rather than the point estimate
Questions whether a 6-hospital UK evaluation transfers to the US pipeline
Proposes edit rate as an observable signal of whether review is actually happening
user_research: Uses the observation study to locate where an error would and would not be caught
Takes the nurses' own stated concern about review effort seriously
prioritization: Weighs one to two quarters of accuracy work against a design change available now
execution: Specifies what is logged and monitored after launch, not only what ships
Builds a path to catch and learn from fabrications in the field
communication: Gives the head of clinical safety the specific thing they asked for
Handles the CEO's investor commitment without letting it set the safety bar

product_sense: Treats 82% vs 91% as the whole question
Optimises for the full time saving in the workflow with no error-correcting layer
analytics: Quotes the 3% fabrication rate as precise
Assumes the UK evaluation transfers to US private hospitals
user_research: Ignores that two of eleven observed handovers had no verbal component
prioritization: Treats model accuracy as the only available lever
execution: Ships with a disclaimer as the only safeguard
Provides no way to detect fabrications after launch
communication: Lets the CEO's investor commitment determine the safety decision

learnTakeaway.title: Design for the error, not just against it
learnTakeaway.body: With probabilistic features, accuracy is one lever and usually the slow, expensive one. The faster lever is what the product does when the output is wrong: whether the user is positioned as an editor or a recipient, whether claims are traceable to sources, whether a wrong answer is easy to notice, and whether you can detect failures after launch. Two failure modes with the same rate can carry completely different risk — an omission a conversation will catch is not the same as a confident fabrication in a written-only workflow.

qaSubmissions.label: strong
qaSubmissions.rationale: 82% against a 91% human baseline is the wrong comparison: humans omit at 9% and fabricate at 0%; the model omits at 15% and fabricates at ~3%. Omissions are survivable — 9 of 11 handovers surfaced them verbally. The 2 of 11 written-only handovers are where a confident false statement lands unchallenged. I wouldn't spend a quarter on accuracy: at 1.4% fabrication the safety position is identical, so the constraint is the interaction. Ship the draft with per-claim provenance, confirmation and edit-rate logging, and treat a falling edit rate as automation bias, not a win.

qaSubmissions.label: defensible_alternative
qaSubmissions.rationale: Ship the reviewed-draft version — provenance and confirmation — to three pilot hospitals for a quarter rather than to everyone. The design is the same one I'd ship broadly and I agree it's what unblocks clinical safety. I'm narrowing because of evidence quality: 400 summaries from 6 similar UK trusts, reviewers agreeing 87% of the time, and a fabrication interval from 1.6% to 5.2%. That's a lab number. I want a field number, and a better answer for the US groups than 'we measured it in England'. The costs are real: the investor commitment slips and ready safeguards wait.

qaSubmissions.label: weak
qaSubmissions.rationale: 82% acceptable against a human baseline of 91% is close enough, and humans make mistakes too. The time saving is 12 minutes per nurse per shift which is 40 hours a week at a mid-size trust, and competitors are already shipping. I would ship it with a clear AI-generated disclaimer telling users to check it, and improve accuracy over time.
